clue.text: Constant criticism curtailed at parting

indicators.note: a curtailed word has had its tail docked, so its final letter goes
something parting is split open, so another piece sits in the gap it leaves

parts.note: STICK is criticism, as in 'taking stick'; docked of its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone endures a constant stream of criticism that only stops when they finally go their separate ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' is British slang for harsh criticism, as in 'taking stick'; 'parting' looks like a farewell but means split apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Something static stays fixed and unchanging, which is what constant means as an adjective.

clue.text: HRT treatment remains open to debate

indicators.note: giving letters a treatment works them over into a different order

parts.note: the three letters rearranged
ash is what remains after burning
out as in flowers out, i.e. open

explanation.surface: Whether hormone replacement therapy is a good idea is still a matter people argue about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open to debate' reads as one phrase, but it splits: OUT is open, 'to' joins, and debate is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrash out an issue is to discuss it thoroughly until agreement is reached, a phrasal verb for arguing it through.

clue.text: Outwit champion concealing sudden move

indicators.note: words that conceal something keep it tucked away inside their own letters

parts.note: runs across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A challenger outsmarts the champion while hiding a surprise move, like a chess game or a bout.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the two words: ou-TWIT CH-ampion.
explanation.definitionFit: A twitch is a brief jerky spasm or motion, a quick involuntary movement of the body.

clue.text: Political activist is able very shortly to take in fool

indicators.note: said shortly, a word is cut short and loses its final letter

parts.note: if you are able, you can

indicators.note: to take something in is to receive it inside, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: the word cut short, its last letter deleted
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A political campaigner briefly manages to dupe somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' joins definition to wordplay; 'very shortly' looks like 'soon' but means the word very with its tail cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: A canvasser goes door to door seeking votes or support for a party or candidate during an election.

clue.text: Very hot yet was composed

indicators.note: to compose is to put together or arrange, so the letters are set out anew

parts.note: six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Despite the heat, someone stayed calm and collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' looks like calm, the opposite of sweaty; it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sweaty describes perspiring heavily, which is how a person feels when overheated.

clue.text: Back copies one acquired are a brownish colour

indicators.note: going back means running the letters the other way round
something acquired is taken in and held, so it ends up inside

parts.note: to ape is to copy, so copies is apes
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Old back issues of a magazine you have picked up have gone yellowy-brown with age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back copies' suggests old issues; really APES turned round to SEPA, which then takes in I.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepia is the reddish-brown tint of old photographs, originally an ink made from cuttlefish.

clue.text: Former lover's not embellished son's excuses

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
plain means unadorned
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: An ex-partner bluntly gives the son's reasons for misbehaving, without any dressing up.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophes are surface glue: EX + PLAIN + S, with 'excuses' a verb, not the son's plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse something, in the sense of justifying it, is to account for it, as when one explains away a mistake.

clue.text: Someone attempting to start off unloading goods

indicators.note: unloading a vehicle means emptying its cargo, so those letters are removed

parts.note: to trigger is to set off or start something
G stands for good, so two goods are GG

explanation.surface: Someone tries to begin emptying a delivery of merchandise from a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goods' looks like freight, but it is the plural of G (good); TRIGGER with both Gs taken out leaves TRIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A trier is a person who makes an effort or has a go, literally one who tries.

clue.text: Strange going back inside Tangier office

indicators.note: something going back travels backwards, so it is read right to left
inside means within, so the letters lie within the run of the clue words

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words, to be read backwards

explanation.surface: Something odd is happening back in an office in Tangier, a Moroccan port.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'taNGIER OFfice' from right to left to find the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Foreign can mean unfamiliar or alien to one's experience, as in an idea quite foreign to me.

clue.text: Fatberg sat about causing alarm

definitions.note: a participle phrase for a base-form verb; the answer means to astonish

indicators.note: about means around in a jumble, so the letters are moved round

parts.note: fat is flab, followed by berg as written
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A fatberg, a huge sewer mass of grease and wet wipes, lodged somewhere and alarmed everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fatberg' reads as one word but must be split into fat and berg, and only fat is replaced by a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To flabbergast is to astonish or stun someone, close to shocking or startling them.

clue.text: Dad swamps kir cocktail with spice

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters are mixed up
what swamps something engulfs it, surrounding it completely

parts.note: papa is a word for father
the drink's letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Father spikes a kir, a French drink of white wine and cassis, with some spice.
explanation.walkthrough: Kir really is a cocktail, so 'cocktail' reads as description; it is the anagram signal, and Dad is the longer form of the word, not the two-letter one.
explanation.definitionFit: Paprika is a red powdered seasoning ground from dried sweet peppers, widely used in Hungarian cooking.

clue.text: Every other change neatly arranged

indicators.note: arranged letters have been put into a new order

parts.note: to alter is to change
the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Swapping every second item round so that everything is tidily ordered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neatly arranged' reads as tidiness, but 'arranged' is telling you to reorder NEATLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something alternately means on each second occasion, taking turns in a repeating pattern.

clue.text: Really disappointed in ugly car parks at oasis

indicators.note: something ugly is misshapen, so the letters lose their tidy form

parts.note: fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A traveller is let down to find hideous car parks spoiling a desert oasis.
explanation.walkthrough: AS SICK AS A PARROT is a British idiom, a cliché of football interviews, for bitterly disappointed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes extreme dejection after a setback, the opposite of being over the moon.

clue.text: Squander money in buffet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to spend recklessly, as in wasting all your wages
second meaning: a buffet is a knock or strike

explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' wants to be a self-service meal where you might overspend; here it is a knock, rhyming with 'tough it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Blow means both to waste cash freely and a hard knock delivered with a hand or by the wind.

clue.text: Perhaps Galileo's maestro or Newton, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several possible arrangements of the letters

parts.note: taken as written
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.surface: Was Galileo's teacher perhaps Newton? A mischievous question about scientific lineage.
explanation.walkthrough: Newton suggests the scientist, who fits the theme, but he is just N, the unit of force named after him. 'Perhaps' flags Galileo as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Galileo studied the heavens with his telescope, making him an example of a scientist of stars and planets.

clue.text: Laughed at reading 1 down — setter had put in funny clue

indicators.note: to put something in is to place it inside, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: reading is one of the three Rs
the Roman numeral for one
D is the abbreviation for down

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters come out strangely ordered

parts.note: the setter is I, and I had contracts to I'D
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A solver mocks the setter after reading 1 down, where a joke clue had been slipped in.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 down' looks like a cross-reference, but this grid has no 1 down; it is just I and D. I'D (setter had) wraps the reordered CLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ridicule someone is to mock or deride them, making them the butt of jokes and scornful laughter.

clue.text: Engineer questions exchanging money for new false reports

indicators.note: to engineer is to contrive or construct, so the letters are built into a different shape
exchanging one thing for another swaps a letter out and puts a replacement in its place

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for money
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An engineer is interrogated about bribery, cash changing hands, and the accounts of it turn out to be untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like a person; it is a verb telling you to rebuild the letters after M replaces the N in QUESTIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Misquotes are inaccurate repetitions of someone's words, so they are wrong or untrue accounts of what was said.

clue.text: Continue protecting cupola, a positive sign for the future

definitions.text: a positive sign for the future

indicators.note: to protect something is to shield it on all sides, so it is surrounded

parts.note: to go on is to continue
a cupola is a small dome

explanation.surface: Keeping a building's cupola safe is taken as an auspicious sign for what lies ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The dome goes in between the second O and the N of GO ON, giving GOO-DOME-N.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a portent of things to come, and a favourable one predicts happy events ahead.

clue.text: Deteriorating swimming resort's losing special quality

indicators.note: swimming things move about freely, so the letters are moved round
losing something means it is gone, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the possessive read as plain letters
S is the abbreviation for special
a grade is a level of quality

explanation.surface: A swimming resort is going downhill and losing what made it special.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimming resort' reads as a lido or spa; the S of RESORTS goes twice, once as the possessive and once for special, leaving REORT to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrograde can mean going backwards or getting worse, describing a decline into an inferior state.

clue.text: Region in Italy certainly covered by motoring organisation

indicators.note: something covered by another has that other wrapped round it

parts.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, a British breakdown service
si is Italian for yes

explanation.surface: A roadside rescue service's cover definitely extends to some area of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Region in Italy' wants to be the definition, say Umbria, but 'in Italy' belongs to the wordplay; Region alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is a continent, the world's largest landmass, so a vast geographical region of the globe.

clue.text: Accounts book's advantage in long run

indicators.note: in places one thing within another, between its outer pieces

parts.note: the first letter of each word
having the edge means having the advantage

explanation.surface: Keeping good books gives a business an advantage over time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the long run' is a stock phrase, but long and run each give only their initial letters, L and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A ledger is the main register in which a business records its financial transactions.

clue.text: Winning fellow in duel chose to turn early

indicators.note: turning letters over and round changes their order

parts.note: a side that is winning is ahead

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: the nine letters rearranged
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A duellist who is winning decides to swing round before the count is up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn early' evokes duellists turning before their paces are done; 'turn' is the anagram signal and early is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done before the planned time or deadline is completed sooner than expected.

clue.text: In France I set up English court in exile

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: je is French for I
E is the abbreviation for English
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Someone from France establishes an English royal court while living abroad in banishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In exile' looks like a state; 'in' only joins, and exile is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To exile someone is to expel or banish them, throwing them out of their country.

clue.text: Stumbled over a slang word for man

parts.note: fell is the past tense of fall, so stumbled
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tripped while saying a colloquial term for a bloke.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so FELL sits on top of A.
explanation.definitionFit: Fella is an informal spelling of fellow, used casually to mean a guy or bloke.

clue.text: Heat-retaining articles worn by soldier left behind

indicators.note: clothes worn by someone are wrapped around them, so they go outside

parts.note: the and a, the definite and indefinite articles
RM is a Royal Marine
L is the abbreviation for left, placed behind, at the end

explanation.surface: Warm underclothes worn by a soldier get left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heat-retaining articles' reads as the definition, thermal underwear; but 'articles' belongs to the wordplay as two grammatical articles.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermal describes something designed to keep warmth in, such as insulated clothing.

clue.text: Lamp's laboriously cleaned out with a soft touch

parts.note: a lamp is a light

indicators.note: a thing cleaned out has had its insides cleared, leaving only its shell

parts.note: only the first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: An old lamp has been painstakingly cleaned with a gentle hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of Lamp's is a link meaning 'is'; LIGHT then the shell of laboriously.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something lightly means using gentle pressure, with delicacy rather than force.

clue.text: Verse has singular beat unknown by leading academic

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for singular
to tan someone's hide is to beat them
in algebra x, y and z are unknowns

indicators.note: the leading letter is the one at the front of the word

parts.note: the first letter

explanation.surface: A poem has a peculiar rhythm that the head of department has never heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like poetic rhythm, fitting verse, but here it means thrash: TAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanza is a group of lines forming a unit in a poem, so a verse in the sense of one section.

clue.text: Compulsion to put on nursing uniform

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close in one's arms, so one piece cradles another

parts.note: to put clothes on is to dress
U is Uniform in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone feels obliged to wear their nurse's uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nursing uniform' reads as a nurse's outfit; 'nursing' actually means holding, and uniform is just U.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress means coercion or threats forcing someone to act against their will.
